migrationNotes: Spine: one timber plank bridging a gap. Follow the stress from the squeezed face to the stretched face, turn that into σ = My/I, learn I for a rectangle, see why standing the plank on edge wins, and finish by moving the material out into an I-section.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): none. Every item is asked.

lesson.title: Bending stress and the I-beam

lead.text: Bend a ruler between your hands and look at its two faces. The face on the outside of the curve gets longer, so that layer of material is stretched. The face on the inside gets shorter, so it is squeezed. Between them there is a layer that keeps its length. The line where it crosses the cross-section is the neutral axis, and in a shape that is the same above and below, like a rectangle, it runs along the middle.

Layers further from the neutral axis stretch or shorten by more, in proportion to their distance from it. We call that distance y, and engineers call each thin layer a fibre. Strain grows with y, and stress is E times strain, so the stress grows with y as well. It is zero at the neutral axis and largest at the outer fibre, the fibre furthest from the axis.
Use what you have just read about where the neutral axis sits in a symmetric section.

Now the stress needs a number. At a distance y from the neutral axis, σ = M × y ÷ I. Here M is the bending moment and I is a property of the cross-section called the second moment of area. A bigger moment or a larger y gives a bigger stress, and a larger I gives a smaller one.

I measures how well the shape of a section resists bending. It is not the area. It counts each bit of area more heavily the further it sits from the neutral axis, so material far out helps a great deal and material near the axis hardly helps. Its unit is mm⁴, because it comes from an area times a distance squared. To get the stress in MPa, turn kN·m into N·mm by multiplying by 10⁶ and use mm for y and mm⁴ for I.

steps.headline: The second moment of a rectangle

lead.text: For a rectangle of width b and depth h, the second moment of area about its neutral axis is I = b × h³ ÷ 12. The depth h is the size measured in the direction of the bending, from the squeezed face to the stretched one. It is cubed, and the width is not. A beam 120 mm wide and 100 mm deep has I = 120 × 100³ ÷ 12 = 10 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

afterFigure.text: Put a moment of 4 kN·m on it, which is 4 × 10⁶ N·mm. The outer fibre is half the depth from the axis, so y = 50 mm and σ = 4 × 10⁶ × 50 ÷ (10 × 10⁶) = 20 MPa. The picture shows this section, and the same section turned to stand 100 mm wide and 120 mm deep.

lead.text: Compare the two orientations of the section on the last screen, and think about what the depth does in the formula.
Work in newtons and millimetres, where 1 kN·m is 10⁶ N·mm. The largest stress is at the outer fibre.

steps.headline: A beam 50 mm wide and 120 mm deep carries 6 kN·m. Find the largest bending stress.

lead.text: Here is the whole method, line by line.

workedSteps.text: The largest stress is at the outer fibre, half the depth from the axis.
Put the moment in N·mm and use σ = My/I.

steps.headline: The same plank is laid flat, 200 mm wide and 100 mm deep, under the same 20 kN·m. Find the largest bending stress.

lead.text: The method is the same as in the worked example.

workedSteps.text: Swap the width and depth in bh³/12.
The outer fibre is now half of 100 mm from the axis.
Use σ = My/I, with M in N·mm, to get the stress in MPa.

lead.text: Compare the two answers for the plank. On its edge, 200 mm deep, the largest stress was 30 MPa. Laid flat, 100 mm deep, it was 60 MPa. Halving the depth cut I to an eighth, and doubling the width brought it back up to a quarter. Meanwhile y halved. A quarter of the I with half the distance leaves twice the stress.

The cube in bh³ ÷ 12 is what makes depth so powerful. Suppose a beam keeps its width and its depth is tripled. I grows by 3³ = 27 times while y only triples, so for the same moment the stress falls to a ninth. Making a beam deeper is a cheap way to make it strong, which is why floor joists stand on edge and why a steel beam is deeper than it is wide.
Cube the depth before you multiply by the width.

The stress is small near the neutral axis, so wood or steel there does little work, yet it still adds weight. A steel I-section puts most of its metal in two wide flanges at the top and bottom, where the stress is greatest. A thin web along the middle joins them. The beam keeps much of the stiffness of a solid one with a fraction of the metal. The picture compares an I-section with a solid rectangle of the same outline.

afterFigure.text: To find I for an I-section, take the outer rectangle and subtract the two empty regions beside the web. Take a section 80 mm wide and 150 mm deep, with 10 mm flanges and an 8 mm web. Each empty region is (80 − 8) ÷ 2 = 36 mm wide and 150 − 20 = 130 mm deep, so I = (80 × 150³ − 72 × 130³) ÷ 12 = 9.32 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The solid 80 × 150 rectangle has 22.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴, so the I-section keeps 41 percent of the stiffness with 22 percent of the area.

lead.text: Find I as the outer rectangle minus the two empty side regions, as on the last screen.

lesson.orientation: Use σ = My/I and see why depth and flanges make a beam efficient.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Take a 100 mm by 200 mm plank from a timber yard and lay it across a gap to make a small bridge. Stand on the middle and it bends a little. Now turn it on to its narrow edge and stand on it again. Wood, span and weight are all the same, yet the plank behaves differently.

The last lesson gave the bending moment at every point along a beam. That says how hard the beam is being bent. It does not yet say how hard the wood is working, and two planks under the same moment can be working very differently depending on the way up they sit and the shape of their cross-section.

This lesson follows the stress through the depth of a beam, from the squeezed face to the stretched one. It ends with a formula that turns a bending moment into a stress, and with a reason why steel beams are shaped like the letter I.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the largest bending stress in a beam, and see why deep sections and I-beams carry bending well.

recap.keyIdea: Bending stress is σ = My/I, zero at the neutral axis and largest at the outer fibre. For a rectangle I = bh³/12, so depth matters far more than width.

blocks.text: Back at the plank, you found 30 MPa standing on edge and 60 MPa laid flat under the same 20 kN·m. You also found that a 200 mm deep I-section keeps about 31 percent of the solid rectangle's I with about 15 percent of its material.

recap.nextHook: A beam that is strong enough can still sag, and a floor that bounces is a failure of another kind. The next lesson works out how far a beam sags and what controls it.

questions.prompt: A 100 mm × 200 mm timber plank is to be used as a floor joist. Which way up makes the stiffer joist?
hints: Think of bending a ruler flat, then on edge.
questions.onCorrect: Standing on edge is stiffer: the depth is cubed in I, and on edge the plank is 200 mm deep.

misconceptions.feedback: Lying flat puts the material close to the middle, where it does little. Try bending a ruler both ways.
Try bending a ruler flat and on edge. The difference is large.

choices.label: Standing on its 100 mm edge, 200 mm deep

acceptedIdeas: Standing on its 100 mm edge, 200 mm deep
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Standing on its 100 mm edge, 200 mm deep. On edge the plank is 200 mm deep, and depth matters far more than width in bending.

questions.prompt: A symmetric section is 120 mm deep. How far, in mm, is its outer fibre from the neutral axis?
hints: Where does the neutral axis of a symmetric section sit?
It is at mid-depth.
Take half of the depth.
questions.onCorrect: 60 mm. In a symmetric section the neutral axis is at mid-depth, so y is half the depth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole depth. The neutral axis is at the middle, so the outer fibre is half of it out.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The neutral axis is at mid-depth, so the outer fibre is 120 ÷ 2 = 60 mm from it.

questions.prompt: A solid rectangular beam 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep carries a bending moment of 20 kN·m. Its second moment of area is bh³/12. Find the largest bending stress, in MPa.
hints: Convert the moment to N·mm: 1 kN·m = 10⁶ N·mm.
The outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis.
questions.onCorrect: 30 MPa: σ = My/I, with the moment in N·mm and y half the depth.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the full depth, 200 mm, for y. The outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis.

questions.prompt: Why is the stress largest at the outer fibre?
hints: What does σ = My/I say about y?
questions.onCorrect: σ = My/I rises with y, so the fibre furthest from the neutral axis works hardest.

misconceptions.feedback: Every fibre carries some load, but those near the neutral axis carry very little.
I is one number for the whole section. It does not change with position.

choices.label: Stress grows with distance from the neutral axis, and the outer fibre is furthest.
The outer fibre carries all of the load.
I is largest at the surface.

acceptedIdeas: Stress grows with distance from the neutral axis, and the outer fibre is furthest.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stress grows with distance from the neutral axis, and the outer fibre is furthest.. σ grows with y, and the outer fibre has the largest y.

hints: Use M = 20 × 10⁶ N·mm and y = 50 mm.
Divide M × y by I.
questions.onCorrect: 60 MPa, double the on-edge value: I falls to a quarter while y only halves.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stress with the beam on edge. Laid flat, I is smaller and the outer fibre is closer.
That keeps y at the old 100 mm. Laid flat, the depth is 100 mm, so y is half of that.

questions.prompt: Find the second moment of area of a rectangle 60 mm wide and 100 mm deep about its horizontal centroidal axis, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴.
hints: Use I = bh³/12 with h the depth.
Cube the depth before multiplying by the width.
Calculate 60 × 1,000,000 ÷ 12, then divide by 10⁶.
questions.onCorrect: 5 × 10⁶ mm⁴: width times depth cubed, over twelve.

misconceptions.feedback: That is I in mm⁴. The question asks in units of 10⁶ mm⁴, so divide by 10⁶.

questions.prompt: An I-section is 200 mm deep with 100 mm wide, 10 mm thick flanges and a 6 mm web. Its I is the outer rectangle minus the two empty side regions: (100 × 200³ − 94 × 180³)/12. Find I in units of 10⁶ mm⁴, to two decimal places.
hints: Each empty region is 47 mm wide; together they are 94 mm wide and 180 mm deep.
Subtract their combined bh³ from the outer rectangle's.
Divide the difference by 12 and by 10⁶.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 × 200³ = 800 × 10⁶ and 94 × 180³ = 548.2 × 10⁶; the difference over 12 is 20.98 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

questions.onCorrect: 20.98 × 10⁶ mm⁴: about a third of the solid rectangle's I, from about a sixth of the material.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the solid rectangle. Subtract the empty side regions first.
That is the difference before dividing by twelve.

questions.prompt: A square beam 100 mm × 100 mm carries 5 kN·m. Find the largest bending stress in MPa.
hints: Find I for the square with bh³/12.
The outer fibre is 50 mm from the axis.
questions.onCorrect: 30 MPa: I for the square, then σ = My/I with y half the depth.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the full depth for y. The outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis.

questions.prompt: A rectangular beam's depth is doubled and its width is unchanged. By what factor does its second moment of area change?
hints: In bh³/12, which letter changes?
What happens to h³ when h doubles?
Multiply 2 by itself three times.
questions.onCorrect: I rises eightfold: depth is cubed, which is why deep sections are so much stiffer.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the factor for doubling the width. Depth is cubed in bh³/12.
That squares the depth. In bh³/12 the depth is cubed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: I = bh³/12, so doubling h multiplies I by 2³ = 8.

questions.prompt: Name the line through a bent beam's cross-section where the bending stress is zero.
hints: Fibres on one side are stretched and on the other squashed. What lies between?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The neutral axis, which passes through the centroid of the section.

questions.onCorrect: The neutral axis passes through the centroid and carries no bending stress.

misconceptions.feedback: That line does sit in the middle, but it has a specific name. What do engineers call the line of zero bending stress?
